  audit adds the operator-facing **decision** for every row. No directive is claimed

## 1. Executive Summary

### 1.0 How To Read The Ledger

Every row has exactly one **decision**: `enforced`, `runtime-owned`, `security-difference`, `behavior-gap`, `out-of-profile`, `fail-closed`. `Catalog` is the committed machine classification; `Decision` is this audit's operator-facing judgment. `Rationale` is generated from the catalog evidence/migration data plus the explicit rule sets in the generator, so a reviewer can audit the rule, not the prose.

### 1.1 Counts Per Decision Category

| Decision | Count | Share | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `enforced` | 111 | 14.9% | the Rust data plane executes the directive and committed evidence asserts the behavior it reaches |
| `runtime-owned` | 131 | 17.6% | the nginx value has no client-visible effect because the Rust runtime owns that subsystem by design |
| `security-difference` | 17 | 2.3% | intentional stricter/safer behavior than nginx, justified by the declared security posture |
| `behavior-gap` | 55 | 7.4% | the value is client-visible behavior the runtime does not produce yet; it is scheduled in the remaining wave-3 backlog |
| `out-of-profile` | 229 | 30.8% | excluded from the declared http-core-v1 product profile (PRD section 4) and rejected in an active context |
| `fail-closed` | 201 | 27.0% | rejected at materialization and not planned, because the feature is outside the declared required surface or unsafe without separate requirements |
| **total** | **744** | **100%** | every inventory row appears exactly once |

**Sum proof:** 111 + 131 + 17 + 55 + 229 + 201 = **744**. The generator fails closed if the sum is not
744, if any row is duplicated, or if a (`module`, `name`) pair is repeated.

### 1.5 Headline Findings

1. **111 of 744 directives (14.9%) are executed by the Rust data plane today**, up from 79 at the first audit snapshot:
   Waves 1, 2, 2b, 3a and 3a-2 landed 32 directives. 131 more are deliberately runtime-owned (17.6%) and 17 are intentional, spec-justified security differences.
2. **55 behavior-gap directives remain in the wave-3 backlog** (7.4% of the surface): HTTP/1 framing policy (1), body addition filter (3), referer module (1), HTTP/2 tuning (14), static open-file cache (3), proxied method override (1), OCSP stapling / trust chain (HTTP) (3), stream module gaps (29).
3. **430 of 744 directives (57.8%) are excluded or rejected, not silently emulated.** 229 are explicit PRD section 4 profile exclusions and 201 are fail-closed rejections outside the planned backlog.
4. **The catalog's previously reported over-claims are resolved.** All 6
   evidence-citation mismatches were replaced with the stronger committed tests and
   all 11 "enforced typed key" migration actions now
   reflect actual materializer consumption; the generator gates both classes so they
   cannot silently regress (section 4.3).
5. **Regenerating this report is mandatory when the catalog moves.** It is a generated
   snapshot of the post-Wave-2b worktree, not a hand-maintained table; section 6 states
   the exact commands and the wave-3 landing procedure.

## 2. Decision Ledger By Module

One row per inventory directive, grouped by nginx group and module (the same grouping the operator matrix uses). Every one of the 744 `(module, name)` pairs appears exactly once; bare names can repeat across modules (for example `listen`, `map`, `proxy_pass`), so the module heading is part of the identity.

### Decision Legend

| Decision | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `enforced` | the Rust data plane executes the directive and committed evidence asserts the behavior it reaches |
| `runtime-owned` | the nginx value has no client-visible effect because the Rust runtime owns that subsystem by design |
| `security-difference` | intentional stricter/safer behavior than nginx, justified by the declared security posture |
| `behavior-gap` | the value is client-visible behavior the runtime does not produce yet; it is scheduled in the remaining wave-3 backlog |
| `out-of-profile` | excluded from the declared http-core-v1 product profile (PRD section 4) and rejected in an active context |
| `fail-closed` | rejected at materialization and not planned, because the feature is outside the declared required surface or unsafe without separate requirements |

Known difference: a map source must be exactly one supported variable (no composite "$host:$port" source); a result variable cannot be the source of another map; `volatile` fails closed; maps are evaluated once before the rewrite loop, so a map sourced from $uri/$document_uri observes the pre-rewrite URI (nginx evaluates lazily at first use); duplicate result variable names fail closed (nginx silently keeps the last declaration). |

## 3. Wave Completion And Remaining Behavior-Gap Backlog

### 3.1 Completed Waves (1, 2, 2b)

The catalog now classifies every directive below as `executable` with committed
evidence. Wave 1 was the routing/static correctness set; Wave 2 added redirect
construction, limit status codes, range ceilings and typed-TOML map/chain materialization;
Wave 2b closed the proxy response-header policy, internal locations, slash merging and
request-header acceptance; Wave 3a added the header-level charset family and the gzip
user-agent/proxied refinements; Wave 3a-2 added the autoindex listing family plus the
empty_gif and stub_status location handlers.

timing, orphan `.gz` sidecars, regex proxy_redirect/cookie forms, and the nginx
pre-vhost-selection `merge_slashes` quirk); those are documented in each catalog entry's
`knownDifferences` and are not counted as backlog rows.

### 3.2 Remaining Behavior-Gap Backlog (wave 3 backlog, 55 directives)

These are the categories `specs/nginx-gap.catalog.json` lists as still open after
Wave 3a-2 (plus the addition filter and referer module the same wave note names as
remaining in this area). An accepted-unenforced row is silently ignored today; a
rejected row fails the configuration load. Both are real migration gaps, so every row carries the
operator-visible loss, the reason it is **not** runtime-owned, the files that would
have to change, and the tests to add.

### 3.3 Backlog Sequencing Note

Within the backlog, the largest operator payoff is the stream module gaps (a whole
transport plane), followed by the HTTP/2 tuning set (configurations that declare HTTP/2
limits are rejected today even though HTTP/2 itself executes). The body addition filter
and the referer module are medium-sized features that pull in a bounded subrequest engine
and `$invalid_referer` variable threading respectively. `proxy_method`,
`chunked_transfer_encoding` and the static open-file cache are smaller, bounded
changes. The OCSP/trust-chain rows are limited by the rustls capability gap recorded as
`tls.ocsp-stapling: missing` in the gap catalog.

Two former backlog rows are **not** remaining gaps and stay accepted-unenforced with
truthful diagnostics: `charset_map` (byte-level transcoding is deliberately out of
scope; the runtime owns charset translation at header level) and `gzip_comp_level` (the
compression layer owns the level).

## 4. Enforced Spot-Check

### 4.1 Method

- A sample of 64 `executable` directive rows was drawn,
  covering the original surface (routing, static content, proxying, cache, limits, TLS,
  stream) **and every directive completed by Waves 1/2/2b/3a/3a-2**.
- For each one the audit **read the cited file** and confirmed the cited
  function/case exists and its assertions cover the behavior the catalog attaches to
  the directive. Mechanical existence is re-checkable offline with
  `node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs --verify-evidence`.
- Verdicts: `verified` means the reference exists and the assertions prove the claimed
  behavior. Section 4.3 records the previously reported over-claims and their current
  state.

**No unresolved over-claim remains.** The two classes reported in the previous snapshot
were fixed and are now gated by `--verify-evidence`:

**A. Evidence-citation mismatches (6, resolved).**
The weak citations were replaced with the stronger committed tests shown below; the
gate fails if any entry regresses back to the old citation.

| `http:ssl_protocols` | `crates/sdkwork-webserver-core/src/nginx/mapping.rs::materializes_ssl_listener_with_certificates` | now cites ssl_protocols_declaration_selects_the_tls_window, which asserts both min and max TLS versions. | resolved |

| `stream:ssl_certificate_key` | `tests/nginx/full-surface/probe.py::case_tls_sni_certificate_selection` | now cites stream_proxy.rs::terminates_stream_tls_and_forwards_plaintext_to_upstream. | resolved |
| `stream:ssl_client_certificate` | `crates/sdkwork-webserver-core/tests/nginx_config_surface.rs::every_supported_directive_family_materializes (case "ssl_verify_client with ssl_client_certificate")` | now cites case "stream ssl terminate with client auth", which asserts stream ClientAuthMode::Required plus the CA list. | resolved |
| `stream:ssl_verify_client` | `crates/sdkwork-webserver-core/tests/nginx_config_surface.rs::every_supported_directive_family_materializes (case "ssl_verify_client with ssl_client_certificate")` | now cites case "stream ssl terminate with client auth". | resolved |

**B. Migration-action over-claims (11, resolved).**
The matrix gate now derives `importer.tomlEnforced` from actual materializer
consumption, so the migration actions no longer promise a typed key that is silently
dropped. The gate asserts that no accepted-unenforced entry claims an unconsumed
"enforced typed key", and that no executable entry renders an accepted-but-ignored key.

| `core:pid` | `pid` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |
| `core:user` | `user` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |
| `core:worker_processes` | `workerProcesses` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |
| `events:worker_connections` | `workerConnections` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |
| `http:error_log` | `errorLog` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |

| `http:sendfile` | `sendfile` | tomlEnforced is now false (accepted-but-ignored diagnostic). | resolved |

One semantic caveat remains explicit rather than silently resolved:
`http:keepalive_timeout` maps to a consumed key, but as `limits.requestTimeoutMs`
(a request timeout, not the keep-alive idle timeout). The catalog records this in
`importer.tomlSemantics` and the migration action says so.

**C. Evidence grade (not an over-claim).** 29 of the
111 executable rows cite only the generic
`every_supported_directive_family_materializes` case. That case does assert the
normalized fields per surface case, so it is mapping evidence, not end-to-end behavioral
evidence. Behavioral proof for those directives rests on the
`tests/nginx/differential-*` batteries and `tests/nginx/full-surface`, which is a
stronger contract than the per-row citation suggests. The catalog could distinguish an
evidence **grade** (`materialized` vs `behavioral`) instead of implying every
executable row has a behavioral test.

### 4.4 Decision Consistency Check

Consistent: `executable` <=> `enforced` in both directions (111 <=> 111). Every completed-wave directive is executable and every executable directive is enforced.

## 5. Why Full Nginx Parity Is Not A Coherent Target

### 5.1 The Audit Data Says So

| Bucket | Directives | Share of 744 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `enforced` (actually nginx-compatible behavior) | 111 | 14.9% |
| `security-difference` (intentionally not nginx) | 17 | 2.3% |
| `behavior-gap` (planned toward compatibility) | 55 | 7.4% |
| `runtime-owned` (deliberately not nginx value) | 131 | 17.6% |
| `out-of-profile` (PRD section 4 exclusion) | 229 | 30.8% |
| `fail-closed` (rejected, not planned) | 201 | 27.0% |

561 of 744 directives (75.4%) are
**not** nginx-behavior compatibility surface by design: the Rust runtime owns the value
(process model, event loop, buffers, timeouts, TLS policy, logging, upstream policy) or the
feature is explicitly rejected. The compatibility program is the 111 executed directives plus the 55 planned backlog; full parity would still have to add every rejected and excluded
feature below.

### 5.2 Out-Of-Profile Groups (229 directives)

- `ngx_core_module` - 1 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_fastcgi_module` - 49 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_geoip_module` - 5 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_memcached_module` - 11 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_perl_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_scgi_module` - 44 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_uwsgi_module` - 61 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_auth_http_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_core_module` - 9 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_imap_module` - 3 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_module` - 1 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_pop3_module` - 2 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_proxy_module` - 7 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_realip_module` - 1 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_smtp_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_mail_ssl_module` - 20 directive(s)
- `ngx_stream_geoip_module` - 3 directive(s)

What implementing each group would actually require:

| Group | Directives | What full parity would require |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| FastCGI | 49 | a FastCGI record-protocol client, request/response stream framing, CGI-variable marshalling, and a security model for app-supplied params; a separate protocol product surface with its own conformance corpus. |
| uWSGI | 61 | the uWSGI packet protocol (modifier1/modifier2), params/body marshalling, and its own upstream TLS/cache policy surface. |
| SCGI | 44 | SCGI netstring framing plus a CGI environment model; same security review as FastCGI. |
| memcached | 11 | a memcached text/binary protocol client and cache-status mapping into the response pipeline. |
| Mail proxy (SMTP/IMAP/POP3 + auth) | 51 | three protocol state machines, STARTTLS, auth backends (HTTP/IMAP/POP3), and a mail-specific security review. |
| Perl | 4 | an embedded Perl interpreter - executable configuration, explicitly excluded. |
| GeoIP | 8 | a MaxMind database dependency plus an OS/database-specific lookup contract. |
| Dynamic module loading | 1 | an ABI/loading contract that the static nginx OSS reference binary does not even provide; conflicts with the standalone-only deployment profile. |

### 5.3 Fail-Closed Groups (201 directives, top modules)

- `ngx_http_proxy_module` - 31 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_grpc_module` - 29 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_core_module` - 16 directive(s)
- `ngx_stream_ssl_module` - 14 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_ssl_module` - 13 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_userid_filter_module` - 9 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_v3_module` - 8 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_image_filter_module` - 7 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_ssi_filter_module` - 7 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_xslt_filter_module` - 6 directive(s)
- `ngx_stream_proxy_module` - 6 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_rewrite_module` - 5 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_browser_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_dav_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_mp4_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_stream_core_module` - 4 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_headers_filter_module` - 3 directive(s)
- `ngx_http_gzip_filter_module` - 3 directive(s)

Representative implementation cost:

| Group | Directives | What parity would require |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| gRPC upstream (`ngx_http_grpc_module`) | 29 | an HTTP/2 gRPC transport with trailers, status mapping, :authority handling, upstream TLS/SNI policy, retry policy - a second proxy protocol family. |
| Rejected proxy knobs (`ngx_http_proxy_module`) | 31 | cache locking/background update/bypass/method sets, body substitution, upstream-trust knobs: each is a bounded policy feature with its own security review. |
| Rejected stream plumbing (`ngx_stream_proxy_module`) | 6 | buffer sizing, TLS library caches/commands/CRL/password-file knobs; the routing/identity subset is instead in the wave-3 backlog. |
| HTTP/2 tuning (`ngx_http_v2_module`) | 0 | the http2_* set is tracked as wave-3 backlog, so this module is expected to move rather than stay fail-closed. |
| TLS extras (CRL/OCSP-response/ECH/ticket files) | 27 | rustls feature gaps (OCSP response handling, raw public keys, certificate compression, session ticket key files) plus a certificate-material pipeline. |
| HTTP/3 + QUIC (`ngx_http_v3_module`, `ngx_quic_bpf_module`) | 9 | a QUIC transport (UDP, TLS 1.3 QUIC keys, connection migration, congestion control) - a separate transport product, explicitly excluded by PRD section 4. |
| Embedded filters (SSI/XSLT/image/mp4/FLV/empty-gif) | 25 | embedded template/language/codec dependencies (libxslt, libgd, mp4/FLV parsers) that the standalone data plane does not ship. |
| `if`/`set` rewrite control (`ngx_http_rewrite_module`) | 5 | a general conditional rewrite interpreter - contradicts the bounded rewrite state machine PRD section 6 requires. |

### 5.4 Lua, njs, And Third-Party Modules

The 744-row inventory is the pristine nginx **OSS tarball** directive table
(`inventory.source.thirdPartyModules` = "excluded (a pristine nginx OSS tarball contains
none)"), so Lua/njs/third-party directives have **zero** rows here even before the profile
decision. They are excluded twice: absent from the inventory, and excluded by PRD section 4
as embedded executable configuration. The reference build's `configureArgs` list
(`--with-http_v2_module`, `--with-http_v3_module`, `--with-mail`, `--with-stream`, and so
on) describes what the differential oracle contains, not what http-core-v1 promises.

### 5.5 Conclusion

A "parity" target would require: five extra application protocols (FastCGI/uWSGI/SCGI/
memcached/gRPC), three mail protocols, a QUIC transport, three embedded languages/filters,
and operator-tunable internals that the Rust runtime replaces by design - while the
deployment profile forbids the stock nginx process those features exist to serve. The
coherent target is the declared `http-core-v1` profile with the four PRD section 2 grades
(parse, semantic, behavioral, operational), a generated directive catalog, and a
versioned evidence revision. That is what this ledger audits.

## 6. Reproduction And Change Control

### 6.1 Commands

```sh
# 1. Regenerate this audit (deterministic; reads only committed inputs).
node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs

# 2. CI freshness gate (exits 1 when the report is stale). Safe to wire in.
node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs --check

# 3. Re-verify the audited claims against the repository sources (offline, read-only).
node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs --verify-evidence
```

The generator reads `specs/nginx-directive-inventory.json` and
`specs/nginx-directive-support.catalog.json`; it makes no network calls, embeds no
timestamps or git HEAD, and sorts every collection before rendering, so a rerun on the
same catalog is byte-identical. `--check` regenerates in memory and compares bytes.

### 6.3 Which Claims Change When Wave 3 Lands

The 55 wave-3 backlog rows are the only behavior-gap
entries that can move to `enforced`. When a wave-3 slice lands, the workstream (or the
Lead) must:

1. Update `crates/sdkwork-webserver-core`, the gateway data plane, tests, and the wave
   notes in `specs/nginx-gap.catalog.json`.
2. Regenerate the catalog + operator matrix via
   `node tools/check-nginx-directive-matrix.mjs --write` (the catalog is generated from
   the implementation by the matrix gate reconciliation).
3. Rerun `node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs` and commit the regenerated report
   with the catalog change; `--check` fails otherwise.

Count effects per moved slice: `behavior-gap` decreases by the slice size,
`enforced` increases by the same size, and the category disappears from section 3.2
once all its rows are executable.

### 6.4 Wiring Suggestion For The Lead

`package.json` is outside this audit's write scope. The Lead can add the two
non-mutating invocations to the release verification chain, for example next to
`check:nginx-matrix`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "check:nginx-directive-audit": "node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs --check && node tools/gen-nginx-directive-audit.mjs --verify-evidence"
  }
}
```

and include `check:nginx-directive-audit` in the `_sdkwork:verify` aggregate after the
catalog/matrix gate. The generator fails closed on a count mismatch, a duplicate row,
an unknown directive in a decision set, a completed-wave classification regression, a
consumed-key claim that no longer holds, a reintroduced weak citation, a missing evidence
file in `--verify-evidence`, or a stale report in `--check`.
